To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cagA‐gene was detected in 70% of the H pylori strains isolated from 60 healthy Chinese adults.

1) The prevalence of H. pylori cagA‐pos strains was high in healthy Chinese adults; 2) The cagA‐neg strains were associated with higher levels of serum anti‐CagA IgG; and 3) The cagE‐neg strains were more frequently detected in H. pylori‐infested patients with duodenal ulcer than in those with gastritis.
the prevalence of cAGA+ strains in healthy, young Chinese adult was high.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the treatment of Helicobacter Pylori.
the development of an effective, safe and low cost treatment of H. pylori infections.
the prevalence of caga‐positive strains in H. pylori‐infested healthy young adults in China.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cagA‐gene‐positive strains of H. pylori are associated with the development of gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease and gastritis, and are also associated with the development and progression of gastric mucosa‐associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma.
the prevalence of celiac disease in the general population of China is unknown and that it is likely to be higher than in other parts of the world.
the presence of cagA in H. pylori is not a marker of disease, but a marker of exposure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of caga‐positive strains is higher in Chinese than in Western populations.
cagA‐negative strains of H. pylori are more prevalent in developing countries than developed countries.
the prevalence of caga‐positive strains in H. pylori‐infested healthy young people in China is high and that the prevalence is similar to those in patients with peptic ulcer disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of cAGA positive strains is high in young, healthy adults.
H. pylori infection is common in young Chinese adults.
H. pylori is a major cause of gastric disease in developing countries, but that the strains are less pathogenic than those found in the West.
